content:
At MR.TATTOO, located in Hanoi Old Quarter, we create custom Maori-inspired and Polynesian-style tattoos based on each customer's ideas, preferred placement and personal style.

1. What Is Maori Tattoo Art?

Traditional Maori tattoo art is known as Tā Moko. It is an important cultural art form of the Māori people of New Zealand. Traditional Tā Moko can represent ancestry, identity, social connections and personal history.

Polynesian tattoo art includes different traditions from Pacific Island cultures. Although these styles share some visual similarities, each has its own patterns, meanings and cultural background.

Today, Polynesian-inspired tribal designs are also popular among people looking for bold, meaningful and distinctive tattoos.

2. Popular Maori & Polynesian Tattoo Designs

Some popular design inspirations include:

  • Tribal Patterns: Bold lines, repeated shapes and geometric compositions.

  • Spearhead Patterns: Sharp, directional elements often used in tribal designs.

  • Ocean & Wave Motifs: Inspired by the sea and the relationship between Pacific Island communities and the ocean.

  • Sun & Natural Elements: Designs inspired by nature and the surrounding environment.

  • Polynesian Geometric Patterns: Repeating shapes arranged into detailed compositions.

Each traditional symbol can have a specific cultural meaning. We recommend understanding the background of a design before choosing it.

3. Maori Tattoo Placement Ideas

Maori-inspired and Polynesian-style tattoos can be designed to follow the natural shape of the body.

Popular placements include:

  • Full sleeve and half sleeve tattoos.

  • Shoulder and upper arm tattoos.

  • Chest and shoulder combinations.

  • Forearm and wrist tattoos.

  • Leg and calf tattoos.

  • Back and full-body compositions.

The arrangement of patterns is important because it helps create a balanced tattoo that follows the body's natural contours.

5. Frequently Asked Questions About Maori Tattoos

Are Maori and Polynesian tattoos the same? No. Maori tattooing belongs to Māori culture, while Polynesian tattoo traditions include several distinct cultural practices across the Pacific Islands.
